title: Plan in five minutes
summary: Turn a task contract and controlling focus into a compact introduction–body–conclusion plan with specific evidence, purposeful transitions and a final coverage check.

sections.title: A plan is a route, not a draft
content: E6.1–E6.4 produced a task contract, usable ideas, an ordered sequence and one controlling focus. A compact plan now records the job of each paragraph and the evidence that will perform that job. It should be detailed enough to guide writing but brief enough to scan while composing.

Do not spend planning time writing polished sentences. Use short notes, arrows and exact examples. If a note does not help satisfy the task contract or advance the controlling focus, remove it before drafting.

sections.title: Use a five-minute rehearsal routine
content: Minute 1: reread the topic, command, audience and scope, then write the controlling focus. Minute 2: give body paragraph one a job and attach one or two specific details. Minute 3: give body paragraph two a different job, attach evidence and decide how it develops the first paragraph. Minute 4: sketch the introduction and conclusion jobs. Minute 5: add relationship words and audit every task requirement.

Five minutes is a NextScholar training target, not a claimed official allocation for the ASEAN Scholarship test. During practice, accuracy comes first; reduce the time only after the routine is reliable.

sections.title: Build the body before the frame
content: Controlling focus: breaking a large task into smaller parts made the charity sale manageable and helped the writer adapt when plans changed. Body 1 job: show the method creating the initial plan. Evidence: divide publicity, supplies, prices and staffing; assign deadlines; notice unfinished work. Link-back: separate tasks turned confusion into manageable action.

Body 2 job: show the same method during disruption. Evidence: rain forces the stalls indoors; rank urgent moving and safety tasks; reassign helpers before handling decorations. Link-back: one-priority-at-a-time thinking supports calm adaptation. The second paragraph develops the first instead of repeating it.

sections.title: Frame the plan with an introduction and conclusion
content: Introduction job: establish the school learning and the different life situation, then state the controlling focus. A plan note such as ‘maths problem-solving method -> charity sale -> manageable decisions and adaptation’ is enough; a full opening paragraph is not.

Conclusion job: return to the central insight, show what the writer learned and, if useful, indicate a credible future application. Do not introduce a new main example or simply repeat the introduction word for word.

sections.title: Make transitions show relationships
content: A transition should tell the reader how the next part relates to the previous one. ‘At first’ opens the initial plan; ‘When conditions changed’ signals a complication; ‘As a result’ marks a consequence; and ‘This showed me’ introduces reflection. Choose the relationship first and the wording second.
Avoid decorating every sentence with connectors. Record one useful transition at the boundary between plan stages, then let the paragraph's evidence and explanation create the rest of the flow.

sections.title: Audit before drafting
content: Run five checks: every task-contract requirement appears; the introduction states one focus; each body paragraph has a distinct point, specific evidence and a link-back; transitions show real relationships; and the conclusion closes the existing response without adding a new centre.

Common failures are drafting instead of planning, listing details without paragraph jobs, repeating the same job twice, using empty transitions such as ‘secondly’ when the relationship matters, and discovering a missing prompt requirement only after writing. Repair the plan now, when moving one note is cheap.

sections.title: Complete the compact plan
content: Make six decisions that turn the E6 focus map into a timed introduction–body–conclusion route. Complete the group before viewing feedback. The target is a usable plan, not polished composition prose.
